Why Plastic Bags Are Good for You - Seriously

The 2009 Keep America Beautiful Survey, run by Steven Stein of Environmental Resources Planning, shows that all plastic bags, of which plastic retail bags are only a subset, are just 0.6 percent of visible litter nationwide.

They surveyed 13 miles of road out of 3.8 million miles of road. That sample size provides a pretty large margin for error when it comes to particular waste levels, considering the ability for plastic films to be transported by wind.

In 2010, according to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Americans threw away 690,000 tons of HDPE bags. Of those, approximately 30,000 tons were recycled. That means a total of 660,000 tons were discarded, mostly into landfills (approximately 82 percent of non-recovered municipal solid waste goes to landfill; 18 percent is incinerated). That same year, Americans also chucked almost exactly the same amount of "reusable" polypropylene bags (680,000 tons), of which zero were recovered. In other words, those polypropylene reusable bags actually constituted a slightly higher proportion of all bags going to landfills.

33 million tons of plastic waste is generate in the US each year, 9% of that is recycled (2.8 million tons). Out of that plastic waste only 14% of plastic films are recycled, the rest is land-filled (85-86%). EPA waste estimates place the figures at 4.78 million tons of HDPE (not exclusively films) and 5.55 million tons of LDPE (primarily films) not recovered. No information is provided to the specifics of HDPE film prevalence in generated waste streams by the EPA that I have seen. Going to need some better citations for their data than what they've provided.

But what about larger-scale impacts, such as climate change? Where do grocery bags stack up there? A 2011 study from the U.K.'s Environmental Agency attempted to quantify the emissions footprint both of plastic bags and of their substitutes. Holding the typical HDPE grocery bag up as the standard, researchers found that the common reusable non-woven polypropylene bag—the ubiquitous crinkly plastic tote, typically made with oil—had to be used at least 11 times to hold its own against an HDPE grocery bag. Cotton bags had to be used an amazing 131 times to do the same.

This is misleading. While non-disposable bags do have a much higher fabrication cost (in the environmental sense), Figure 5.1, their long term impacts (used 173 times) are far lower than those of single use plastic film bags (used once), Figure 5.2.

You would have to sit down and measure how many times a plastic bag can be used to determine it's comparative viability to that of non-disposable bags. Then to get that viability you would also have to convince people to actually reuse their plastic bags when they go shopping. US consumers make roughly 1.6 trips a week to the grocery store now. That means that after 87 weeks, the non-disposable bag has been used at least 173 times, a little over a year and a half to break even. Continued usage of that bag will result in drastically lower CO2 equivalency ratings. Similarly reuse of plastic bags also reduces their CO2 impact. Invariably the question becomes one of economy of scale.

This is the same argument for building quality concrete roads versus lower quality asphalt roads. Long term gains supersede short term ones.

In April, NPR's Planet Money reported on the economics of plastic recycling, and noted that while recycled plastic from bags and sacks was once a profitable industry, times have changed.

Plastic bags have not been profitable for recycling in the past. Only recently have recycled films started to become viable on the commodities market. Even while they're at a price point above aluminum and scrap steel the handling and inefficiency for transporting, and the difficultly associated with recycling plastic films makes them unappealing for the recycled commodities industry as a whole. It requires specialized machinery and lots of hand labor to process the plastic bags since waste stream processing roller systems and grinders get easily jammed by them, halting the entire plant's operations and costing millions in repairs. Additionally not all plastic films get recycled.

A 2011 survey published in the journal Food Protection Trends found coliform bacteria in fully half of the reusable shopping bags tested in a random survey of shoppers in Arizona and California. The same 2014 Edelman Berland study that found consumers frequently forgot their bags also unearthed the fact that only 18 percent of shoppers reported cleaning their bags "once a week or more." An article in the Journal of Infectious Diseases traced a 2010 outbreak of norovirus to nine members of an Oregon soccer team who had touched or eaten food stored in a contaminated reusable bag.

Plastic bags which are contaminated are no more or less safe than non-disposable ones.

TLDR: Biased article is biased.

Take away: Recycling plastic bags is good and we should do more of it instead of throwing them into landfills.

They were moving at a Regan Marathon pace, too; not brisk. I couldn't get it out of my head that the potato was walking the dogs from a scooter. My heart rate spiked and I needed to slow down to stay in the zone. I reached my distance goal, turned around, and started running back. In the distance I heard a fat voice- you know the kind, Simply Sara sort of semi-retarded sounding because the fat bulges their cheeks and tongue? Anyway, I heard it repeating "close! close!" Like, stay close to me, not close the door. I was mystified until I rounded the corner and started approaching the potato from behind. The dogs were not on leashes.

The dogs were unleashed. Let me tell you, that is something notable in my city. We have specific off-leash parks where dogs can be socialized and can play. Running paths chock full of runners and bikers are not those places. Sometimes the paths go through off-leash parks, but this path was a path jammed between the river on one side and the zoo or chain link fence or a major road on the other; there was no park. Now, I want to emphasize that despite their owner being a potato, the dogs were nice, harmless, non-aggressive, and well-groomed. The potato was apparently willing to risk its dogs' impoundment (or injury, given the bikes), for reasons I couldn't fathom.

I passed the potato and its dogs. No problems. Then I hear the potato start barking "close! close!" It took me a minute to realize what was happening- I didn't bother looking back. The dogs, apparently so bored with following a potato, were trailing along behind anyone going faster and/or smelling interesting (like physical effort instead of yeast, for example). The potato was shouting at them to trigger training that kept them from getting too far away. I wasn't worried about the dogs; they'd proven they were even-tempered already. I just felt so bad for them.

Then about a km later I realized that the spot I'd encountered the potato was, at minimum, two or three km from the nearest residential area. The potato wouldn't feel tired from the scootypuff, but those poor dogs with their tiny legs would. Why would the potato scoot that far from food? Why would it keep the dogs in pretty adequate condition when it couldn't handle the same for itself? Why would it risk running out of scootyjuice so far from easy calories? How did it manage to get the dogs trained and socialized when it wouldn't let them get more than 15 feet away from its horrible form? Why did it think it was okay to clutter my beautiful running path with a battery-powered potato that had no access to portal guns?

These questions haunt me to this day.

HAPPY ENDING: a couple days later I saw another potato, probably in his late 60s, jogging down another section of the same path. I screamed encouragement at him. He smiled shyly and kept going. I hope he makes it.
